name: Adinkra
basis: why: symbols stamped in dark ink in squares on cloth; how: symbol per square sized by tone, uneven ink pressure
note: The symbol system is the tradition; stamping (carved calabash stamps) is the process.

lumenary.blurb: Symbols of the Akan people of Ghana, stamped in dark ink on cloth. Each one carries a saying, such as the heart, the fern, the ram’s horns. They grow larger and heavier where your picture is dark.

facts.from: The Akan peoples of Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire

why: Adinkra symbols are visual sayings. Each one stands for a proverb or a value: the heart for patience and tolerance, the fern for endurance, the ram’s horns for strength and humility. They are stamped in dark ink in squares on cloth, so a cloth is a page of sayings, and here the symbols grow larger and heavier where your picture is dark.
how: Carry ten symbols drawn with strokes and fills: rings, heart, sankofa, horns, star, fern, twist, comb, handcuffs and tree.
Divide the cloth into squares with three-line rules made with a comb, as on the real cloth.
In each square read the shade v of the picture, its darkness on light cloth or its brightness on dark cloth, and stamp a symbol sized by v.
Add the ink’s slight uneven pressure and let the picture tint the cloth.
Choose ink from bark brown, picture colour or gold, on cream, indigo, red or ochre cloth.
history: Adinkra cloth was first worn at funerals, and the word is often given as meaning goodbye. Symbols are carved into pieces of calabash and stamped on cotton with a dark dye boiled from tree bark. Tradition links the name to Nana Kwadwo Agyemang Adinkra, a king of Gyaman. Symbols such as Sankofa, which says to go back and fetch what you forgot, are now used on buildings, jewellery and logos.
uses: Educational material about proverbs and values
terms: A set of symbols of the Akan people, each carrying a saying.
A symbol and saying about learning from the past.
A gourd, here carved into stamps.
paragraphs: Adinkra cloth comes from the Akan peoples of Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire. Symbols are carved into pieces of calabash and stamped onto cotton with a dark dye boiled from tree bark. The cloth was first worn at funerals, and the word is often given as meaning “goodbye”. Each symbol carries a saying: the heart of patience and tolerance, the fern of endurance, the ram’s horns of strength and humility. The program carries ten of them (rings, heart, sankofa, horns, star, fern, twist, comb, handcuffs and tree), drawn with strokes and fills and cut with small details.

The cloth is divided into squares by three-line rules made with a comb, as on the real cloth. In each square the program reads the shade v of your picture, which is its darkness on light cloth and its brightness on dark cloth, and stamps a symbol whose size grows with v. Very light squares are left bare. Since a stamp’s area grows as the square of its size, the ink on the cloth rises quickly with darkness, which gives the picture its depth. The ink is never even: its opacity is multiplied by a fine noise, so some of it is thin or missing, as with a real stamp.

equations.note: Half the stamp size: s is the square size and f the size-follows-shade slider.
The share of a square covered by ink, for filled symbols.
Uneven inking: the alpha of the stamped layer is scaled by a noise n of wavelength about 5 px.
A multiply blend with strength β = 0.7 × the tint slider, which dyes light cloth with the picture. Indigo and red cloth use a screen blend at 0.35 instead.

presets.text: Gold ink on indigo looks like a festival cloth.
Strong shading makes the symbols follow the picture closely.
Fewer rules leave the symbols open.
